title: Factcheck: No, Europe is not having its ‘quietest’ year for wildfires - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief factchecks viral claims by Matt Ridley, Matthew Wielicki and Bjorn Lomborg that 2026 is Europe's quietest wildfire year, showing the charts rely on a GWIS dataset in which Russia is 74% of the area and 80-90% of burned area. EU-only EFFIS data shows nearly 435,000ha burned as of 29 July - second only to 2022 - with France setting a modern record and Spain running at five times its seasonal average.

themes.theme: Dataset choice as a misinformation mechanism

insights.claim: Charts circulating from prominent climate sceptics that appear to show 2026 as Europe's quietest wildfire year rely on the Global Wildfire Information System definition of Europe, which includes the whole of Russia.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A textbook case of geographic aggregation distorting a headline metric - apply the same scrutiny to any regionally aggregated climate or commodity dataset used in a market argument.
insights.locator: These charts all use data from the Global Wildfire

insights.claim: Russia accounts for about 74% of the land area in the GWIS definition of Europe and typically 80-90% of its burned area, so a quiet Russian season mechanically masks an extreme season in western Europe.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: One country dominates the index by construction; disaggregate to EU-only EFFIS data before drawing conclusions about European fire risk or insured losses.
insights.locator: As a result, Russia accounts for about 74%

insights.claim: GWIS monitors all fires including deliberately lit agricultural burns, a declining practice across much of Europe, whereas EFFIS filters using land-cover data specifically for forest fires - producing a spurious downward trend in the GWIS series.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A structural downward bias from declining crop burning is being misread as declining wildfire risk; use EFFIS for forest-fire exposure, not GWIS.
insights.locator: Another difference between the two datasets

insights.claim: Calum Cunningham of the University of Tasmania's Fire Centre calls the sceptic claims highly misleading because they aggregate fire activity across an enormous and climatically diverse region.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Expert framing to reuse: spatial aggregation across heterogeneous climates is the specific analytical flaw, not merely a political disagreement.
insights.quote: A relatively quiet season in Russia can easily mask an exceptionally active season in France or Spain.
insights.locator: Dr Calum Cunningham, a research fellow

insights.claim: Matthew Wielicki continued posting GWIS-based charts even after acknowledging that including all of Russia, including vast areas of Siberia, is not a good proxy for Europe.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals deliberate rather than accidental data misuse from an official now leading the US Global Change Research Program - a marker of the coming US federal climate-data posture.

themes.theme: Sceptic messaging entering government and mainstream media

insights.claim: Matthew Wielicki, a former University of Alabama geochemist and self-described professor in exile who has claimed the science is not settled on climate change, was recently appointed by the Trump administration to lead the US Global Change Research Program.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Personnel is policy: US federal climate assessment output and its underlying data choices are likely to shift, raising the value of independent EU datasets like EFFIS.

insights.claim: Matt Ridley, who sits on the academic advisory council of the Global Warming Policy Foundation - a UK climate-sceptic lobby group that refuses to disclose its funders - posted the claim that 2026 is the quietest year for wildfires in Europe by some distance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Tracks how an opaquely funded lobby network seeds a data claim; expect the same pattern around energy-policy datasets in UK debate.
insights.quote: 2026 is the quietest year for wildfires in Europe by some distance

insights.claim: The claim was amplified by Richard Tice of Reform UK, Jacob Rees-Mogg and other prominent rightwing figures, and Ridley repeated it in the Spectator and Daily Mail, moving it from social media into mainstream print.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: UK climate-policy risk is being shaped by an amplification chain running from Twitter to national newspapers to a rising political party - relevant to UK net-zero policy durability.

insights.claim: Ridley was responding to a Daily Telegraph column by Tim Stanley headlined that climate change is real and the right needs to get serious about it, indicating an active split within the political right on climate.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A visible fracture on the right over climate reality; watch whether centre-right outlets diverge from the sceptic wing on energy policy.
insights.quote: This is no longer a matter of speculation: the wildfires of Europe, pitiless and persistent, are the way we live now.

insights.claim: Bjorn Lomborg has also shared similar GWIS-based charts implying European wildfires are declining.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Indicates the misleading chart spread across the full spectrum of climate-lukewarmer commentary, not just hard sceptics.

insights.claim: EU burned area as of 29 July 2026 was almost 435,000 hectares according to EFFIS - second only to 2022 for this point in the year.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Hard number for sizing 2026 European wildfire loss exposure: a top-two season year-to-date, relevant to reinsurance, utilities and forestry.
insights.locator: Looking at the EU-only data from EFFIS

insights.claim: France broke its previous cumulative annual burned-area record in the third week of July by more than 19,000ha, and by 29 July was nearly 24,700ha above the previous record with fires still burning.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: France has set a modern record with the season unfinished - direct read-through to French insured cat losses and forestry/agriculture exposure.
insights.locator: The third week of the month saw France

insights.claim: France's wildfire season was only slightly above average for much of the first half of 2026 before a notable uptick in the first week of July, showing how fast the record was set.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Season-to-date benignity is not predictive; European fire risk can go from average to record in roughly three weeks.
insights.locator: For much of the first half of the year

insights.claim: Spain's burned area as of 29 July had almost matched its previous record for this point in the year and is nearly five times the average for the date, tracking among the worst since EFFIS records began in 2006.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Iberian fire exposure is running at five times normal - watch Spanish insurers, grid infrastructure near Madrid and agricultural output.

insights.claim: More than 220,000 people were evacuated due to the Gironde fire west of Bordeaux in what may be France's largest peacetime evacuation, while nearly 90,000 were forced from homes in central Spain.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Displacement at this scale forces emergency fiscal spending and political response - a near-term catalyst for European adaptation budgets.
insights.locator: More than 220,000 people have been evacuated

insights.claim: A record-breaking June heatwave dried out vegetation across the region beforehand, allowing the July fires to spread quickly - a sequential heat-then-fire mechanism.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Heatwave data is a leading indicator for fire loss with roughly a one-month lag; usable for positioning ahead of European fire seasons.

themes.theme: Political reframing of wildfire as security risk

insights.claim: A joint UK/Spain government statement declared that this summer's wildfires demonstrated climate change is now a national security emergency facing Europe and threatening our way of life.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reclassifying climate as national security unlocks defence-adjacent budget lines and faster procurement - watch for firefighting aviation, resilience and monitoring contracts.
insights.quote: This summer’s wildfires demonstrated that climate change was now a national security emergency facing Europe and threatening our way of life.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the UK, French and Spanish governments

insights.claim: French president Emmanuel Macron convened a crisis cabinet meeting on 27 July over fires ravaging south-west France, and Spanish prime minister Pedro Sanchez called the fires a painful expression of climate change.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Top-level political ownership of the fires raises the probability of new national adaptation spending packages in France and Spain.
insights.locator: On 27 July, French president Emmanuel Macron

insights.claim: Cunningham and colleagues note evacuation orders protect lives but make it more likely houses and structures burn because no one remains to defend them - a second-order trade-off that raises property losses.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Successful life-safety policy can mechanically increase insured property losses; a structural reason European fire loss ratios may worsen faster than fatality counts suggest.
